title: airport botanical gardens
content:
a place for both stillness and movement

I have a soft spot for airports and gardens.

airports — as liminal spaces, neither here nor there, but portals for intersecting journeys, a central node for all the departures and arrivals happening, simultaneously.

gardens — as living containers for ongoing, organic processes. gardens as refuge, as spaces for magic, as responsive micro-cosm of the cosmos, holding spaces for both stillness and movement.

so, you can imagine my delight when I discovered, mid-transit from Shanghai to Istanbul, an airport tropical garden at Hamad International Airport in Doha, Qatar — it’s called “The Orchard.”

I was there last Friday for a very brief layover. I spent most of it here, and I didn’t want to leave. I could feel my body absorbing nutrients from my pores, my energy exhaling everything it had absorbed.

  

it felt like the opposite of an airplane. it was open and spacious. there was bird sounds playing from speakers, and mist sprayed every 10 minutes. the sounds seemed real enough that I had to double check that there weren’t actually birds.

it seemed like something out of an architectural dream — it was so clearly “designed” — with its concrete open seating (with bountiful charging outlets), winding pathways, little hidden nooks, and grassy areas with wooden structures for napping or resting. there was both a “nesting” feeling and an open spaciousness.

   

at the same time, despite how intentionally curated it was — I still felt like there was something almost “wild” about it.

maybe it’s the lushness and biodiversity of plant life, and the fact that such an impressive garden demands extensive care. or the fact that the mist being sprayed every 10-15 minutes actually does make you a bit damp — not just pretend damp.

there were clear paths and structures in this garden — but within these structures, there was so much… life. it didn’t feel overly manicured. nothing felt fake.

people inhabited this garden, took off their shoes and laid down and closed their eyes. they seemed entirely different here, than they did at the gates or airplanes — more… human?

   

perhaps, what most impressed me was that it acknowledged the both/and, simultaneously.

yes, this is an airport, and thus it has the conveniences of an airport. it’s open to the public, without being overwhelmingly crowded. it’s not a $75 airport lounge with a 2 hour maximum stay. it’s an environment/experience, given as a gift to the public.

there was a poreousness in the boundary between the garden and the airport. it felt both contained/nested and spacious/open. it’s designed for both quiet seclusion and accessibility. you could let go — as in, disappear into this garden — and, at the same time, you’re not totally lost in it; it’s not a maze. you’re not worried about missing your flight, because you could walk out of it in 60 seconds or less.

  

how do you create spaces that allow for such stillness, and calm — and, at the same time, such ease of motion? how can you make it open to the public?

of course, I’m thinking about both digital and physical spaces. I want to build spaces that feel like this, spaces which make me want to linger — in contemplative silence — and, which, simultaneously, carry me to new adventures onwards.
